input.rationale: Grounded the mechanism that keeps the two sides' committed content apart after healing in the source that decides it, rather than leaving it as the applied-state receipt's inference. The conflict scan in appendEntries walks the incoming entries, looks each one up in the follower's own store at the same index, and truncates the suffix only when the incoming term differs from the stored term; type and data are never compared, and an incoming entry whose index is at or below the follower's last index with a matching term joins neither the truncation branch nor the append list. A stored LogConfiguration entry at index 118 and an incoming LogCommand at the same index therefore agree as long as their terms are equal, which is what the applied-state receipt records: the restarted side kept its LogConfiguration at 118, the peer kept its LogCommand there, both applied through 121, and a client entry committed afterwards reached every instance. I register that as a behavior tied to the receipt it explains; the open audit continues, and the boundary cases still worth an execution are the fault and storage model ones (a disk-backed commit-tracking store, crash timing, and the same partition observed through a snapshot transfer or a post-healing election).

knowledge.statement: appendEntries reconciles a follower's log with the leader's by comparing terms only: for each incoming entry whose index is at or below the follower's last log index it reads the follower's own entry at that index and deletes the suffix from that index only when the two terms differ, never comparing entry type or data, and an incoming entry whose term matches is neither truncated nor counted among the new entries to append. Two entries at the same index with the same term but different type or content therefore both survive, each side keeping its own, and the follower's applied state keeps the value of its own stored entry.
knowledge.conditions: Follower handling an AppendEntries RPC whose entries overlap the indices it already holds; the leader's and the follower's entries at the shared index carry the same term. Exercised in receipt 8c866b71bf0e470e900a15e895b2bed9, where the restarted side's store held a LogConfiguration entry at log index 118 and the first peer's a LogCommand entry at that index while both sides applied through 121; the truncation branch is reached only through a term mismatch, so it is not a substitute for reconciling content.

knowledge.statement: NewRaft re-derives Raft's own configuration from configuration-carrying log entries only for indices above max(lastSnapshotIndex, lastApplied); the other writers of r.configurations are snapshot restore, snapshot install and the leader's own appendConfigurationEntry path, and nothing else repairs it.
knowledge.conditions: Startup reconstruction in NewRaft over a log store; lastApplied may already be advanced by restoreFromCommittedLogs or by a restored snapshot; configuration entries are identified by LogConfiguration or the deprecated peer entry types.

knowledge.statement: restoreFromCommittedLogs reads the commit index from a CommitTrackingLogStore, clamps it to the last log index, sets the commit index and calls processLogs, which applies the committed prefix to the FSM and sets lastApplied to that commit index; this happens after snapshot restore and before NewRaft's configuration scan.
knowledge.conditions: Config.RestoreCommittedLogs enabled and the log store implements CommitTrackingLogStore; the tracked commit index is at least the index of a configuration entry stored in the log.

knowledge.statement: The configuration a node holds decides its own participation and support arithmetic: runFollower declines to campaign when latestIndex is zero or the local ID has no vote in the latest configuration, a candidate needs quorumSize() votes of the latest configuration, and the leader's commitment is constructed from the latest configuration, so a stale or empty reconstruction directly changes which support is required and counted.
knowledge.conditions: The configuration is the one reconstructed at startup or later written by a snapshot install or a configuration change; quorumSize and the commitment are computed from configurations.latest.

knowledge.statement: appendEntries processes configuration entries only for the entries it newly appends; entries already present at the same index and term are skipped, so ordinary replication from a healthy leader does not re-derive the configuration of a follower whose log already matches.
knowledge.conditions: Follower handling a normal AppendEntries whose entries are duplicates of its own log; entries that are in the leader's compacted prefix instead arrive as an InstallSnapshot, which rewrites both configurations from the snapshot metadata. knowledge.statement: A restart with Config.RestoreCommittedLogs enabled over a commit-tracking log store reconstructs a configuration that is not the one recorded in the node's own log whenever the tracked commit index covers that node's last configuration entry, in both directions and across five exercised shapes: the no-snapshot case reported latest_config_index 0 with no servers against a single-voter entry at log index 1; the snapshot-then-remove case reported the snapshot's two voters, one of them the peer removed at log index 103, against the single-voter entry there; the snapshot-then-promote case reported one voter, the promoted peer still carried as a nonvoter, against the two-voter entry at log index 104; the demote/promote ladder reported one voter against committed entries of three voters and of five voters; and a peer that had snapshotted itself while still a voter reported three voters after its vote had been removed in the committed configuration, where it holds none. The public GetConfiguration view reported the same value, and the flag-disabled controls and the within-flag case whose configuration entry sits above the replayed prefix all reconstructed the entry's own index and voter count.
knowledge.conditions: NewRaft restart over the same log, stable and snapshot stores; RestoreCommittedLogs enabled and the log store implements CommitTrackingLogStore; the node's last configuration entry is either inside the applied prefix replayed from the tracked commit index (divergence, in either direction) or above it (correct reconstruction); the snapshot that supplies the wrong configuration may have been taken by the leader or by the restarting peer itself; no membership change is issued after the restart.

knowledge.statement: In the retained campaign execution a peer that holds no vote in the configuration recorded in its own log acquired leadership on its own initiative: it had snapshotted itself while still a voter (snapshot_config_voters 3), its vote was then removed in the committed configuration (log_config_voters 2, stale_has_vote false), and after both it and the other instance were restarted with the former leader down it reconstructed three voters, campaigned without any external request, and became Leader (campaign_result at parsed index 40: stale_config_voters 3, stale_became_leader true, state Leader) with the other instance — whose own reconstruction held no configuration at all (responder_config_voters 0) — answering one pre-vote and one real vote request from it. The flag-disabled control reconstructed the committed two-voter configuration, held no vote there, sent no request at all and stayed Follower.

knowledge.statement: LogCache wraps a LogStore and forwards five required methods plus a MonotonicLogStore shim (IsMonotonic delegating to the underlying store), but it defines no StageCommitIndex and no GetCommitIndex, so a LogCache value never satisfies CommitTrackingLogStore even when the store it wraps does.
knowledge.conditions: The wrapped store implements CommitTrackingLogStore; the wrapper is constructed with NewLogCache and used as the log store of a Raft instance; the interface set of LogCache is fixed at compile time and does not depend on the wrapped value.

knowledge.statement: With RestoreCommittedLogs enabled, restoreFromCommittedLogs type-asserts the log store to CommitTrackingLogStore and returns ErrIncompatibleLogStore when the assertion fails, logging "restore committed logs enabled but log store does not support it" with the store's Go type; NewRaft returns that error, so a node whose log store is a LogCache over a commit-tracking store cannot start at all, and the message points at the cache type rather than the capable store underneath. Wrapping is not required for the flag to work: the same underlying store used directly passes the assertion, as the package's own test with InmemCommitTrackingStore shows.
knowledge.conditions: Config.RestoreCommittedLogs true and Config's log store is a LogCache wrapping a store that does implement CommitTrackingLogStore; the failure is a startup error returned by NewRaft, not a runtime behaviour. The package documents that the flag requires a CommitTrackingLogStore and that Raft fails to start otherwise, so this is a fidelity gap between the provided wrapper and the provided optional interface rather than an undocumented consensus path.

result.summary: The applied-state receipt is now carried by a source-grounded behavior instead of only by the measurement. Reading the conflict scan in appendEntries (raft.go 1522-1600, material append_new) shows reconciliation is decided by term alone: for each incoming entry at or below the follower's last index the follower reads its own entry at that index and deletes the suffix only when the terms differ, never comparing type or data, and a term-matching incoming entry is neither truncated nor appended. So a stored LogConfiguration entry and an incoming LogCommand at the same index both survive when their terms agree - exactly what receipt 8c866b71bf0e470e900a15e895b2bed9 records (LogConfiguration vs LogCommand at index 118, both sides applied through 121, a later client entry applied by every instance, and conflict_index 0 in the flag-disabled control). Effects: one knowledge created; validated (valid true, execution_requested false). I also note that the controller declined a bounded-completed stop request, so the audit stays open and the next executions worth running remain the fault and storage boundary cases: a disk-backed commit-tracking store, crash/restart timing, and the same partition observed through a snapshot transfer or a post-healing election.

knowledge.statement: LogCache wraps a LogStore and forwards five required methods plus a MonotonicLogStore shim (IsMonotonic delegating to the underlying store), but it defines no StageCommitIndex and no GetCommitIndex, so a LogCache value never satisfies CommitTrackingLogStore even when the store it wraps does.

knowledge.statement: With RestoreCommittedLogs enabled, restoreFromCommittedLogs type-asserts the log store to CommitTrackingLogStore and returns ErrIncompatibleLogStore when the assertion fails, logging "restore committed logs enabled but log store does not support it" with the store's Go type; NewRaft returns that error, so a node whose log store is a LogCache over a commit-tracking store cannot start at all, and the message points at the cache type rather than the capable store underneath. Wrapping is not required for the flag to work: the same underlying store used directly passes the assertion, as the package's own test with InmemCommitTrackingStore shows.

The package documents that the flag requires a CommitTrackingLogStore and that Raft fails to start otherwise, so this is a fidelity gap between the provided wrapper and the provided optional interface rather than an undocumented consensus path.

knowledge.statement: A leader accepts a client membership change as soon as its own latest configuration is committed and it has committed an entry in its term (configurationChangeChIfStable), then computes the new configuration with nextConfiguration from configurations.latest and the request, appends it, immediately installs it as the latest configuration and rebuilds the leader's commitment from it; the request's prevIndex, when nonzero, is the only guard against acting on a different configuration than the caller expected.
knowledge.conditions: The node is leader and its configurations.latest is the one reconstructed at startup rather than the configuration recorded in its log; a client calls AddVoter, AddNonvoter, DemoteVoter or RemoveServer with prevIndex 0 (the package's AddPeer and RemovePeer helpers use 0, and callers may too); the gate does not consult the log's own configuration entry.

knowledge.statement: Because the appended configuration entry is immediately the leader's latest configuration and the leader's commitment is rebuilt from it, the quorum that commits a membership change is the reconstructed one, not the committed configuration's quorum: with a reconstruction that has fewer voters than the committed configuration, a change can be committed with support that is not a majority of the configuration being replaced and can include a peer that is not in it, and the peers of the committed configuration that the reconstruction no longer counts as voters are not asked for support at all.
knowledge.conditions: A node whose reconstruction is smaller than the committed configuration leads; a client membership change is issued to that leader with prevIndex 0; the reconstruction keeps the other peers as members so replication can still reach them. Exercised in receipt 2caa49e2796e4a19884ddafd38610f91: the change committed with the leader and a fresh instance as the only voters of the new configuration, while the configuration entry in the leader's own log named three voters.

knowledge.statement: In the retained client-change execution the committed membership was rewritten without the replaced configuration's majority: the leader had reconstructed one voter against the three voters recorded at log index 106 in its own log, its client AddVoter with prevIndex 0 completed (change_committed true), and its configuration afterwards had two voters — itself and the fresh instance, which was not part of the replaced configuration — with the two peers that had held votes there carried as nonvoters. Both of those peers, restarted with the flag disabled, adopted the rewritten configuration (demoted_peers_adopted 2) and held no vote in it (demoted_peers_with_vote 0), while with the flag disabled the same node could not be leader with the others down, the change failed with "node is not the leader" and both peers kept their votes.

knowledge.statement: In the retained partition execution the reconstruction produced two leaders in the same term with disjoint quorums: the restarted node led on its single-voter reconstruction while the two peers it was partitioned from led on the committed three-voter configuration, both sides committed a uniquely named entry (both apply calls returned success), the first side's configuration named one voter against the second side's three, and neither side's log store contained the other side's entry (cross_entries_seen 0), so the cluster held two committed histories. With the flag disabled the same partition left the restarted node unable to lead with only one of the committed configuration's three voters reachable and produced a single leader.

knowledge.statement: In the retained healed-partition execution the cluster converged on leadership but not on content: after the connections were restored it held exactly one leader (leaders_after_heal 1, parsed index 49) and that leader was the restarted side, at term 4, yet both divergent committed entries were still present, the restarted side's own entry in its store and the other side's entry in theirs (first_entry_survives true, second_entry_survives true, entries_surviving 2); the flag-disabled control ended with one leader as well, the restarted side a follower at term 3 and only the entry that had been committed there (entries_surviving 1 at parsed index 52). The two entries had been written at the same index while both sides held the same term, so each side's AppendEntries treats the other's entry as a duplicate rather than a conflict.

knowledge.statement: In the retained healed-partition applied-state execution two state machines held different committed values for the same log index while the cluster kept serving clients: with the flag enabled the restarted side's store and the first peer's store still disagreed at log index 118 after healing - the restarted side held a LogConfiguration entry there and the peer a LogCommand entry - both sides had applied through index 121 (restarted side applied 121, the minimum applied position of the two peers 121; the first side's own payload at 119, the second side's at 118), and a client entry applied after healing committed at index 121 and was applied by the restarted instance and by both peers (post_heal_payload_on_first_side_fsm 1, post_heal_payload_on_second_side_fsm 2, heal_leader_present true), so ordinary replication after healing carried the cluster forward over the conflict without reconciling it. With the flag disabled the same measurement reported no disagreeing index (conflict_index 0), applied positions of 119 on both sides and the single committed entry.
knowledge.conditions: Three-voter committed configuration recorded at log index 106 while the restarted node's snapshot metadata carries a single-voter configuration; the partition case's conditions, in which the restarted side leads on its reconstruction with a fresh instance beside it while the two peers of the committed configuration lead on their own, both sides committing a uniquely named entry in the same term; the connections are then restored in both directions and one further client entry is applied with a 1500 ms timeout by whichever instance is in Leader state, after which the case compares the two stores over their shared range, reads both sides' applied positions and searches each instance's FSM for the payloads. The healed leader in this receipt was the peer side (first_side_state Follower, first_side_term 4), and the observation window is 1600 ms of healing plus 800 ms after the new commit.

knowledge.statement: appendEntries reconciles a follower's log with the leader's by comparing terms only: for each incoming entry whose index is at or below the follower's last log index it reads the follower's own entry at that index and deletes the suffix from that index only when the two terms differ, never comparing entry type or data, and an incoming entry whose term matches is neither truncated nor counted among the new entries to append. Two entries at the same index with the same term but different type or content therefore both survive, each side keeping its own, and the follower's applied state keeps the value of its own stored entry.
knowledge.conditions: Follower handling an AppendEntries RPC whose entries overlap the indices it already holds; the leader's and the follower's entries at the shared index carry the same term. Exercised in receipt 8c866b71bf0e470e900a15e895b2bed9, where the restarted side's store held a LogConfiguration entry at log index 118 and the first peer's a LogCommand entry at that index while both sides applied through 121; the truncation branch is reached only through a term mismatch, so it is not a substitute for reconciling content.
